title: Opening, date and reception
short: The fifth of Brooke's '1914' war sonnets, drafted as 'The Recruit' in late 1914 and made famous by Dean Inge's Easter sermon and Brooke's death in April 1915.
body: Brooke served with the Royal Naval Division at Antwerp in October 1914 and trained at Blandford Camp, Dorset, where he began this sonnet; a pencil draft at King's College, Cambridge, is titled 'The Recruit'. The five sonnets appeared in the quarterly New Numbers (no. 4, dated December 1914) and in 1914 and Other Poems (1915). On Easter Sunday, 4 April 1915, Dean W. R. Inge read it from the pulpit of St Paul's. Brooke died of sepsis on a French hospital ship off Skyros on 23 April 1915, and the poem became the classic statement of idealistic sacrifice. The opening conditional calmly imagines the speaker's death and directs how he is to be remembered.

title: Sonnet form
short: A hybrid sonnet: Shakespearean octave (ababcdcd) and Petrarchan sestet (efgefg), with the turn at 'And think' (l. 9).
body: The octave rhymes ababcdcd and the sestet efgefg (away/less/given, day/gentleness/heaven), combining the English and Italian sonnet patterns. The octave concerns the body, the 'dust' that will enrich foreign soil; the sestet, after the volta at l. 9, concerns the heart and spirit, purified and returned to the 'eternal mind'. Both parts repeat the imperative 'think', so the whole sonnet is an instruction to the reader on how to mourn. The words 'England' and 'English' occur six times, an insistence that later readers have found either moving or chauvinistic.

anchor: some corner of a foreign field
title: some corner of a foreign field
short: The grave abroad becomes English territory; Brooke himself was buried in an olive grove on Skyros, and the lines became a standard war epitaph.
body: The conceit is that the soldier's buried body claims the ground it lies in for England, a patriotic version of the idea that the dead become part of the earth. The phrase was soon realised literally: Brooke was buried on the Greek island of Skyros on 23 April 1915, and the poem is inscribed on his grave. The lines were widely used on headstones and memorials, and were read at funerals of soldiers throughout the war. 'For ever England' converts a moment of death into permanence and possession.

title: In that rich earth a richer dust
short: The body returns to dust (Genesis 3:19), but this dust is 'richer' because England formed it: biblical mortality turned into national pride.
body: The line builds on the biblical sentence on Adam, 'for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return' (Genesis 3:19), and the burial service's 'earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust'. Brooke plays on 'rich': the foreign earth is already fertile, but the English dust is 'richer', enriched by everything England gave it. Readers have found the comparative either a fine conceit or an unconscious national arrogance. 'Concealed' turns the grave into a hiding place for treasure.

title: A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware
short: England is a mother who gave birth to, formed and educated the speaker; 'whom' gives the dust a person's dignity.
body: England is personified as a mother (feminine 'her' throughout) who 'bore, shaped, made aware' the speaker: birth, upbringing and education in a single rising sequence of verbs. The personal pronoun 'whom' for dust is unusual and makes the remains a person still. 'Gave, once, her flowers to love, her ways to roam' recalls the pastoral England of the Georgian poets, Brooke's own circle, and of his 'Grantchester'. The pause around 'once' hints at the brevity of a life cut short.

title: A body of England's, breathing English air
short: The body is England's possession, made from English air, rivers and sun: nature as both nurse and sacrament.
body: The speaker's body belongs to England ('A body of England's'), formed by its air, 'washed' by its rivers and 'blest' by its suns. The verbs have religious overtones (washing as baptism, blessing), so that nature performs the rites of a national church. Critics have noted that this is the idealised landscape of southern England, gentle and rural, quite unlike the trench landscapes of later war poetry. 'Suns of home' (plural) suggests the many summers of a life.

title: And think, this heart . . .
short: The volta: from the buried body to the purified heart, which death has freed of 'all evil'.
body: The sestet repeats 'think' from l. 1 but moves from body to soul. The 'heart', with 'all evil shed away', recalls Christian ideas of purification at death and the Platonic idea of the soul freed from the body. The syntax is complex: 'this heart . . . no less / Gives somewhere back the thoughts by England given'. Brooke's letters around this time speak of the war as a cleansing, a mood also found in the first sonnet of the sequence, 'Peace', with its 'swimmers into cleanness leaping'.

anchor: A pulse in the eternal mind
title: A pulse in the eternal mind
short: The soul becomes one beat in a universal mind, a Platonic or pantheist afterlife close to Shelley's Adonais.
body: The idea that the dead are absorbed into a cosmic intelligence recalls Neoplatonism and especially Shelley's elegy for Keats, Adonais (1821), where the dead poet 'is made one with Nature' and becomes 'a portion of the loveliness / Which once he made more lovely' (stanzas 42-43). Brooke, a Cambridge Apostle and admirer of the Romantics, fuses this with Christian heaven in the last line. 'Pulse' makes the eternal mind a living body, keeping the sonnet's physical imagery.

sources.cite: P. B. Shelley, Adonais (1821), stanzas 42-43, Project Gutenberg text of Shelley's Complete Poetical Works
Geoffrey Keynes, ed., The Poetical Works of Rupert Brooke (London: Faber, 1946), '1914' sonnets

title: Gives somewhere back the thoughts by England given
short: The soul repays what England gave: the poem is a cycle of gift and return between nation and individual.
body: The line completes a pattern of exchange: England 'bore', 'gave' and 'washed' the speaker; now the heart 'gives somewhere back' the thoughts it received. 'Somewhere' keeps the afterlife indefinite. The list that follows ('Her sights and sounds; dreams happy as her day; / And laughter, learnt of friends; and gentleness') makes Englishness a matter of domestic and social happiness rather than military glory; the poem nowhere mentions fighting, the enemy, or killing.

title: under an English heaven
short: Heaven itself is English: both the English sky and an afterlife imagined in national terms.
body: The closing phrase is deliberately double: 'heaven' is the English sky under which friends laughed, and the Christian heaven to which the soul goes. The ending thus completes the sonnet's identification of England with the sacred. For many readers in 1915 this was consoling; later readers, after the Somme and Owen and Sassoon, often found it complacent. Either way, the sonnet's calm, untroubled cadence is part of its meaning: death is imagined without pain or horror.

title: Reception and critique
short: Hugely popular in 1915 and after, the sonnet was criticised early by Charles Sorley as sentimental; later war poets defined themselves against it.
body: The poem's fame was almost immediate. Dean Inge praised its pure and elevated patriotism in his sermon at St Paul's on 4 April 1915, and Brooke's death three weeks later, followed by Winston Churchill's tribute in The Times, made him a national symbol. Not all soldier-poets agreed: Charles Sorley, killed at Loos in October 1915, wrote that Brooke had clothed his attitudes in fine words but had 'taken the sentimental attitude'. Owen's 'Anthem for Doomed Youth' and Sassoon's satires are often read as replies to this kind of idealism. The imperative 'think only this' asks the reader to exclude every other thought, including grief.
